name: Treaty of Brétigny
summary: After the English victory at Poitiers (1356) and the capture of French King John II, France agrees to the Treaty of Brétigny: England gains full sovereignty over Aquitaine (Guyenne and Gascony), Calais, and other territories, roughly a third of France. John II's ransom is set at three million gold écus. Edward III renounces his claim to the French throne. The peace is the high-water mark of English territorial gains in France, but its terms prove unenforceable; within a decade Charles V of France has recovered most of the ceded territories through diplomatic and guerrilla warfare.

_quarry.structural_significance: Represents the maximum English territorial achievement of the Hundred Years' War's first phase; the ransom of John II drains French royal finances; Edward III's tactical genius and the longbow's tactical dominance reach their culmination; the subsequent French recovery under Charles V demonstrates the limits of military conquest without administrative control
